title: Holding on to hope
def: Hope is the sense that things can get better and that your actions matter; in hard times it grows from small, doable steps and from people who stand with you.
look: a next step you can take in the next hour
someone you are doing this for
a past hard time you came through
use: Pick one small task, finish it, and notice it; remember who is waiting for you; let someone help carry the load.
not: Do not mistake a dark hour for the end of the story; if hopelessness turns to thoughts of dying, reach out now.
call: Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Facing fear of dying in a crisis
def: In a life-threatening moment, fear of dying is natural; turning attention to the next useful action and to people you love can steady you.
look: an urge to freeze or flee
use: Breathe slowly, focus on the next step to stay safe or call for help, and, if it helps you, use your own prayer, words, or silence.
not: Do not give up on the practical steps; most people in frightening situations survive.
call: Call 911 or use satellite SOS if your life is in danger.

title: Forgiveness
def: Forgiveness is choosing to let go of resentment or self-blame so it no longer runs your life; it does not mean excusing harm or returning to danger.
look: a relationship you want to mend
use: Name the hurt honestly, decide what you need to be safe, and let go in your own time and way, whether by prayer, writing, talking, or quiet.
not: Do not force yourself to forgive on a schedule or stay near someone who is harming you.

title: Living with uncertainty
def: Many traditions teach separating what you can change from what you cannot; acting on the first and accepting the second eases worry.
look: worry about things far outside your control
a list of what is in your hands today
use: Write what you can and cannot control, act on one thing you can, and set the rest down for now.
not: Do not mistake acceptance for giving up on safety steps.

title: Small rituals for remembering someone
def: A small ritual, such as lighting a light, sharing stories, writing a letter, or a moment of silence, can help people honor someone when a full service is not possible.
look: the person's own customs or faith
use: Gather those who want to take part, share memories, and use words from the person's tradition or your own.
not: Do not pressure anyone to join or to use religious words they do not hold.

title: If someone dies in the field
also: what to do if someone dies
def: If someone dies outdoors, the first steps are to call for help, keep yourself and others safe, and leave the scene as it is for authorities.
look: a scene that may still be dangerous
use: Call 911 or use SOS, start CPR if trained and it is not clearly too late, mark the location, keep others safe and warm, and take a quiet moment if you wish.
not: Do not move the body unless the place is dangerous, and do not touch weapons or evidence beyond what safety needs.

title: Quiet and awe in nature
def: Spending quiet time outdoors, noticing sounds, light, and the land, is a simple way many people find calm and perspective.
look: a few minutes without the phone
sounds and changes you start to notice
use: Sit for a few minutes, breathe, and notice what you see and hear; return to the same place over days.
not: Do not sit alone somewhere unsafe, near cliffs or water, or without telling someone where you are.

title: Making hard decisions by your values
def: When choices are hard, naming what matters most to you, such as safety, family, honesty, or faith, helps you decide and live with the outcome.
look: two choices that both cost something
use: Get safe first, list your options, ask which fits what you value most, and talk with someone you trust if time allows.
not: Do not let fear or exhaustion make a choice you would not make rested, if you can wait.

title: Finding purpose after a loss
def: After a major loss, many people slowly rebuild purpose through caring for others, honoring the person they lost, and small daily commitments.
look: wanting to do something in the person's memory
use: Start with one small commitment, help someone else, and give yourself time.
not: Do not judge yourself for how long it takes.
call: If the emptiness includes thoughts of not wanting to live, Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Rest and a day of rest
def: Many faiths and simple wisdom set aside regular rest; stepping back restores energy and judgment for the long haul.
use: Plan a regular pause, even a few hours, and protect it for sleep, quiet, family, or worship as you choose.
not: Do not skip rest during long emergencies; tired people make dangerous mistakes.

title: Reading scripture or classic wisdom texts in Yehsa
def: Yehsa carries several public-domain texts, including the King James Bible, the Tao Te Ching, the Bhagavad Gita, the Dhammapada, and Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, which you can ask about by name or topic.
look: asking for a book and chapter
asking what a text says about a topic
quotes shown as what the text says, not a verdict
use: Ask what a named text says about a topic, for example 'What does the Tao Te Ching say about water?'; Yehsa quotes matching lines without interpreting them, and some topics find no passage.
not: Yehsa is not a chaplain and does not debate faith; follow your own tradition and leaders.

title: Courage when afraid
def: Courage is acting on what matters while still afraid; fear often shrinks once you take the first step.
look: a clear next step that frightens you
fear that grows the longer you wait
use: Breathe, name the step, and take it; ask for help or company if you can.
not: Do not confuse courage with taking unnecessary risks.

title: Respecting different beliefs in a group
def: In a mixed group, people may want prayer, silence, or no religious words at all; inviting rather than assuming keeps everyone included.
look: customs around food, rest, or the dead
use: Ask what people want, offer a moment of silence that everyone can use their own way, and respect customs where you can.
not: Do not press beliefs on someone who is hurt, grieving, or frightened.

title: Helping others as a source of strength
def: Helping others after a disaster or in daily life gives purpose and connection, and it strengthens the helper too.
look: neighbors who live alone or are ill
official volunteer channels after a disaster
use: Check on neighbors, share skills or supplies, and volunteer through organized groups rather than self-deploying into danger zones.
not: Do not exhaust yourself or enter hazardous areas to help without training.

title: Patience through a long wait
def: Long waits, for rescue, power, or news, wear people down; structure, small goals, and company make time more bearable.
look: the urge to take risks to end the wait
use: Set a routine for the day, take turns on watch or tasks, conserve energy, and check news at set times.
not: Do not leave a safe shelter just because waiting is hard.

title: Writing down what went right
def: Writing a few lines each day about what went right or what you are thankful for can lift mood and help you see progress.
look: a small notebook or the phone's notes
use: Each evening write three things that went well and one thing you did that helped.
not: Do not use it to deny real problems; note them too and plan for them.
